title: HE MURDERED SEVENTY BROTHERS TO BECOME KING… BUT ONE BROTHER ESCAPED TO DELIVER A WARNING THAT WOULD HAUNT HIM UNTIL DEATH
paragraphs: HE MURDERED SEVENTY BROTHERS TO BECOME KING… BUT ONE BROTHER ESCAPED TO DELIVER A WARNING THAT WOULD HAUNT HIM UNTIL DEATH

The terrifying story of Abimelech: When family becomes a stepping stone to power, ambition becomes an idol, and the blood you shed to build your kingdom becomes the testimony against you. — Judges 9:1–57
There is something deeply frightening about a person who can look into the eyes of his own family and see nothing but obstacles.
Not brothers.
Not people who shared his father's blood.
Not human beings with names, memories, and futures.
Just obstacles.
And sometimes, the most dangerous person in a family is not the one who openly hates everyone.
It is the one who knows exactly how to make betrayal sound like loyalty.
He knows which relatives to approach. Which insecurities to awaken. Which promises to make. Which words will turn family affection into political support.
He doesn't begin by holding a sword.
He begins by winning hearts.
And by the time everyone realizes what he truly wants, innocent blood has already been spilled.
This is the story of Abimelech.
But before you dismiss him as another ancient villain, consider something uncomfortable.
The spirit of his ambition is not confined to ancient history.

It still appears wherever people sacrifice relationships for recognition, manipulate others for personal advantage, or convince themselves that getting what they want justifies what they must destroy.
And there is a question buried inside this terrible chapter of Scripture that every human heart needs to face:
What are you willing to destroy to become the person you desperately want to be?
Because Abimelech's tragedy did not begin when seventy men were murdered.
It began when one man's desire for power became more important than the lives standing between him and his throne.
And the ending?
The ending is so devastating that even the man who thought he could control everything could not control how his own story would be remembered.
Before Abimelech ever approached his mother's relatives, his father Gideon had already been given an extraordinary opportunity.
After the Lord delivered Israel from Midian, the Israelites asked Gideon and his descendants to rule over them.
Gideon answered:
"The LORD shall rule over you." — Judges 8:23, KJV
Those words mattered.
Israel's deliverance had come from God, not from the greatness of a human dynasty.
Yet Gideon's household carried contradictions of its own.
He had many wives and seventy sons. He also had a concubine in Shechem who bore him a son named Abimelech (Judges 8:30–31).
His name is striking.
In Hebrew, אֲבִימֶלֶךְ (Avimelekh) means "my father is king."
What an unsettling name in a family whose father had publicly refused hereditary kingship.
The text does not tell us exactly why Gideon gave him that name, and we should not pretend to know his private intentions.
But the literary irony is impossible to ignore.
The son whose name spoke of kingship would eventually pursue kingship through bloodshed.
And after Gideon died, Israel once again turned away from the Lord.
Judges 8:33 records that the Israelites returned to worshiping the Baals, making Baal-berith their god.
They forgot the Lord who had rescued them.
They failed to show covenant kindness to Gideon's household.
And into that spiritually compromised environment stepped Abimelech.
He traveled to Shechem, the city connected to his mother's family.
He approached his maternal relatives with a proposal carefully designed to sound reasonable.
Why should all seventy of Gideon's sons rule over the people when one man could lead them?
And wasn't he their own flesh and blood?
Judges 9:2 records his appeal:
"Remember also that I am your bone and your flesh." — KJV
In Hebrew, the expression is:
עַצְמְכֶם וּבְשַׂרְכֶם
Atzmekhem uvesarkhem.
"Your bone and your flesh."
These were words of kinship.
Words that should have inspired responsibility, protection, and faithfulness.
But Abimelech used family identity as leverage for personal ambition.
He was not simply asking them to recognize a relationship.
He was persuading them to take his side.
And they did.
His mother's relatives repeated his words to the leaders of Shechem, and their hearts inclined toward him because they regarded him as their brother (Judges 9:3).
Think about that.
They were moved by the fact that he belonged to them.
But they apparently failed to ask what kind of man they were empowering.
How often does something similar happen today?
A relative demands loyalty while behaving dishonestly.
A leader asks for trust while refusing accountability.
Someone invokes family, friendship, ministry, or shared history to silence legitimate questions.
And people follow because the relationship feels more important than the truth.
But belonging to the same family does not make evil righteous.
Sharing the same blood does not excuse shedding innocent blood.
And loyalty that requires participation in wickedness is not biblical faithfulness.
It is compromise.
Then came the money.
Judges 9:4 says the leaders of Shechem gave Abimelech seventy pieces of silver from the house of Baal-berith.
Money associated with an idolatrous sanctuary was placed into the hands of a man pursuing a violent political ambition.
With it, Abimelech hired worthless and reckless men who followed him.
The Hebrew description includes the words רֵיקִים וּפֹחֲזִים (reqim ufochazim), conveying the idea of empty, reckless, or irresponsible men.
He purchased the services of men willing to advance his cause.
And then he returned to his father's house in Ophrah.
What happened next is among the darkest moments in the entire book of Judges.
Abimelech murdered his brothers, the sons of Jerubbaal, on one stone.
Seventy brothers were targeted.
One survived.
The youngest, Jotham, escaped because he hid himself.
The other sixty-nine were killed.
Scripture describes the slaughter with terrible restraint.
No elaborate emotional commentary.
No dramatic speeches from the victims.
Just the cold reality of brothers murdered by their own brother.
On one stone.
Imagine the silence afterward.
The household that once held the voices of Gideon's sons had been devastated.
Men who might have married, raised children, cared for their families, and lived out their own callings were gone.
And why?
Because Abimelech wanted a throne.
Not because God had commanded him to kill them.
Not because they had been convicted of some crime.
Not because Scripture records that they had attacked him.
He eliminated them as rivals to his ambition.
And there is a painful lesson here.
When power becomes your god, people eventually become expendable.
A person does not have to commit murder to reveal the same underlying temptation.
Sometimes it appears in a smaller but still destructive form.
A sibling is cheated out of an inheritance.
A family member is slandered to secure control over property.
An employee is destroyed through lies so someone else can receive a promotion.
A church member is humiliated because another person cannot tolerate correction.
A friendship is sacrificed because reputation matters more than honesty.
These actions are not morally equivalent to mass murder, but they can spring from the same sinful root: the willingness to harm others to protect the self.
James 4:1–2 asks where conflicts and quarrels come from and points toward disordered desires that wage war within us.
The Bible does not merely expose the violence of Abimelech.
It challenges the desires that can grow in any human heart when left unrepented.
And perhaps the most heartbreaking detail is what happened immediately after the slaughter.
The leaders of Shechem and the house of Millo gathered and made Abimelech king near the oak of the pillar in Shechem (Judges 9:6).
He got what he wanted.
The throne.
The title.
The recognition.
The public ceremony.
For a moment, wickedness appeared to have succeeded.
And isn't that one of the hardest things to understand about life?
Sometimes the dishonest person gets promoted.
The manipulator gets applauded.
The betrayer gets the inheritance.
The cruel person gains influence.
And the innocent are left wondering whether justice has disappeared.
You may know that feeling.
Maybe someone in your family took what rightfully belonged to you.
Maybe you were betrayed by a person you defended for years.
Maybe someone told a convincing story about you, and people believed it without hearing your side.
You watched the person who wounded you move forward as though nothing had happened.
And you were left carrying consequences you never chose.
The story of Abimelech does not promise that evil will always be exposed quickly.
But it does reveal something essential.
Human applause cannot transform wickedness into righteousness.
A crown cannot cleanse bloodstained hands.
And a public victory is not proof of God's approval.
While Abimelech was being celebrated, one surviving brother remained.
Jotham.
The youngest.
The one who escaped.
The one Abimelech failed to silence.
When Jotham heard what had happened, he stood on Mount Gerizim and addressed the people of Shechem.
He told them a parable about trees seeking a king.
First, the trees asked the olive tree to rule over them.
The olive tree refused to abandon its productive purpose.
Then they approached the fig tree.
It refused to abandon its sweetness and good fruit.
Then the vine.
It refused to abandon the wine that brought cheer.
Finally, the trees approached the bramble.
And the bramble accepted.
In Judges 9:15, the bramble said:
"If in truth ye anoint me king over you, then come and put your trust in my shadow." — KJV
What a picture.
A bramble offering shade.
A thorny plant promising security.
Something incapable of providing the protection it advertised.
And if the trees would not submit, fire would come out of the bramble and devour the cedars of Lebanon.
Jotham was exposing the foolishness of the people who had crowned Abimelech.
They had rejected the principles of faithful leadership and embraced a man whose ambition threatened to consume them.
Then Jotham confronted them with the blood of his brothers.
Had they acted truthfully and sincerely toward Gideon's family?
Had they repaid Gideon's service with righteousness?
Or had they rewarded a deliverer's household with slaughter?
His warning was severe.
If their actions were righteous, let them rejoice in Abimelech.
But if not, let fire come from Abimelech and consume the leaders of Shechem, and fire from Shechem consume Abimelech.
Then Jotham fled.
He had no army.
No throne.
No political machinery.
Only the truth.
And for a time, the truth seemed powerless.
Three years passed.
Three years in which Abimelech continued ruling.
Three years in which the families of the murdered brothers had to live with what had happened.
Three years in which the guilty appeared to enjoy the rewards of their conspiracy.
But Judges 9:23 records a turning point.
God sent an evil spirit between Abimelech and the leaders of Shechem, and their relationship turned into treachery.
The Hebrew word רוּחַ (ruach) can mean spirit, wind, or breath depending on context. Here the expression describes an evil or harmful spirit sent in judgment.
The passage presents the breakdown of their alliance as part of God's judgment, not as random political misfortune.
And Judges 9:24 explains why.
The violence against Gideon's seventy sons was to be avenged upon Abimelech and the leaders who had strengthened his hands to kill his brothers.
God had not forgotten.

That does not mean every betrayal or disaster in our own lives can be confidently identified as a specific act of divine punishment. Scripture does not authorize us to make that judgment about every tragedy.
But in this particular account, God explicitly reveals His judicial purpose.
The men who had joined together through wickedness began turning against one another.
The alliance built on blood could not sustain peace.
Shechem's leaders became hostile.
Political unrest spread.
Gaal son of Ebed challenged Abimelech's authority.
Zebul, an official loyal to Abimelech, maneuvered against Gaal.
The city descended into conflict.
Eventually, Abimelech attacked Shechem, defeated its inhabitants, destroyed the city, and sowed it with salt.
The man who had gained power through the support of his mother's people became the destroyer of those same people.
The family connection he had exploited became part of a relationship consumed by violence.
Jotham's warning was unfolding.
And then came an even more terrifying scene.
The leaders associated with the tower of Shechem gathered inside the stronghold of the temple of El-berith.
They were seeking refuge.
Abimelech cut branches, placed them against the stronghold, and set it on fire.
About a thousand men and women died (Judges 9:46–49).
The man who had once used silver from a sanctuary associated with Baal-berith to finance his rise now burned people sheltering in a stronghold associated with El-berith.
His pursuit of power had become a catastrophe.
And still, he did not stop.
He marched against Thebez.
There was a strong tower in the city, and the people fled inside.
Abimelech approached the entrance, intending to burn it just as he had done before.
Perhaps he expected another victory.
Perhaps he believed the method that had worked at Shechem would work again.
But this time, someone was waiting above.
Not a king.
Not a general.
Not a celebrated warrior.
A woman whose name Scripture does not record.
She dropped an upper millstone on Abimelech's head and crushed his skull.
The ruler who had ordered the killing of his brothers on one stone was struck down by another stone.
And as he lay dying, his concern turned toward how his death would be remembered.
He called his young armor-bearer and told him to draw his sword and kill him so people would not say that a woman had killed him.
The young man obeyed, and Abimelech died.
Even at the edge of death, Abimelech was trying to control his reputation.
And the irony is devastating.
He could command his armor-bearer.
But he could not command Scripture.
He could arrange the final blow.
But he could not erase the woman who had crushed his skull.
His attempt to protect his pride became part of the very account that preserved his disgrace.
And Judges 9:56–57 gives the divine interpretation of the ending.

"Thus God rendered the wickedness of Abimelech, which he did unto his father, in slaying his seventy brethren: And all the evil of the men of Shechem did God render upon their heads: and upon them came the curse of Jotham the son of Jerubbaal." — KJV
The final word did not belong to Abimelech.
It belonged to God.
But there is something else we must understand before we turn this story into a simple warning about bad people receiving punishment.
If we read Judges 9 only to condemn Abimelech, we may miss the deeper confrontation with our own hearts.
Because the central danger is not merely the desire to become a king.
It is the desire to become our own god.
To control everything.
To be above correction.
To treat other people as instruments of our personal advancement.
To protect our image even when our conscience is pleading with us to repent.
Maybe you have never destroyed someone's life through physical violence.
But have you ever destroyed someone's reputation to protect your own?
Have you ever wanted someone else to fail because their success made you feel small?
Have you ever justified dishonesty because you believed you deserved more?
Have you ever called something God's blessing simply because you finally got what you wanted?
Those questions are not meant to equate ordinary failures with Abimelech's crimes.
They are meant to expose the dangerous direction of unrepented sin.
Jesus taught in Mark 7:21–23 that evil actions proceed from the human heart.
And that is why the Gospel must do more than improve our outward behavior.
It must transform us from within.
Abimelech pursued kingship by killing his brothers.
Jesus Christ, the true King, came to save His people by laying down His own life.
Look at the contrast.
Abimelech manipulated his relatives into supporting his ambitions.
Jesus said that He came not to be served but to serve, and to give His life as a ransom for many (Mark 10:45).
Abimelech destroyed lives to secure his throne.
Jesus surrendered Himself to death to redeem sinners.
Abimelech tried to preserve his reputation as he died.
Jesus endured the shame of the cross for the joy set before Him (Hebrews 12:2).
Abimelech was driven by the need to take.
Christ revealed the love of God through His willingness to give.
Philippians 2:6–8 describes the humility of Jesus, who did not exploit His divine status for selfish advantage but took the form of a servant and became obedient unto death, even death on a cross.
And in the Greek text of Philippians 2:8, we find the expression:
ἐταπείνωσεν ἑαυτὸν
Etapeinōsen heauton.
"He humbled Himself."
What Abimelech refused to do, Jesus willingly did.
Abimelech exalted himself and fell.
Christ humbled Himself, and God highly exalted Him (Philippians 2:9).
This is not merely a lesson about leadership.
It is a revelation of the kind of King our souls desperately need.
A King who does not exploit the weak.
A King who does not demand that the innocent die to protect His sinful ambitions.
A King without sin, who willingly bears the penalty of sin for those He came to save.
And here is the beauty of the Gospel.
The story of Abimelech tells us that wickedness matters and judgment is real.
The cross tells us that God has not abandoned sinners to hopelessness.
Jesus did not die because sin was insignificant.
He died because sin was so serious that reconciliation with a holy God required a sacrifice we could never provide for ourselves.
At Calvary, God's justice and mercy are not enemies.
Christ bears sin, and forgiveness is offered through Him.
The Greek word χάρις (charis) means grace, favor, or gift, depending on its context.
Ephesians 2:8–9 teaches that salvation is by grace through faith, not a reward earned through human works.
And the Greek word μετάνοια (metanoia) refers to repentance—a turning of mind and heart that leads away from sin and toward God.
Real grace does not give us permission to continue manipulating, exploiting, or destroying people.
It calls us to abandon the throne we have built for ourselves and surrender to Jesus Christ.
Maybe your story is not one of murder or political betrayal.
Maybe your story is a family torn apart by money.
A relationship shattered by pride.
An inheritance dispute that turned siblings into enemies.
A marriage wounded by selfishness.
A friendship destroyed by jealousy.
Or years of pretending to be spiritually strong while quietly feeding bitterness.
You may be the person who was wounded.
Or you may be the person who caused the wound.
Sometimes the hardest confession is not, "Lord, look what they did to me."
It is, "Lord, look what I have allowed to grow inside me."
And if that is where you are today, do not hide behind religious language.
Come to Jesus.
Confess what is true.
Turn away from the sin you have been defending.

Where possible and appropriate, make restitution, seek reconciliation, and take responsibility for the harm you caused. Forgiveness does not remove the need for justice or wise boundaries, and reconciliation cannot be forced upon someone you have harmed.
But do not believe that your past has placed you beyond the reach of Christ's mercy.
Consider another man in Scripture.
Saul of Tarsus.
He approved of Stephen's death and persecuted the church (Acts 8:1–3).
He carried authority to arrest followers of Jesus.
He was convinced that his actions were justified.
But on the road to Damascus, the risen Christ confronted him.
And the persecutor was transformed into a witness of the Gospel.
The man who had once tried to destroy the church became the apostle Paul, proclaiming the very Christ he had opposed.
Paul later wrote:
"Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners; of whom I am chief." — 1 Timothy 1:15, KJV
That does not mean Paul escaped every consequence of his past.
It means the mercy of Jesus was greater than the sinful identity that had once defined his life.
And that is the difference between the tragic trajectory of Abimelech and the redemptive testimony of Paul.
Abimelech's account shows a man who continued in destructive ambition until judgment overtook him.
Paul's testimony shows what Christ can do when a sinner is confronted, humbled, forgiven, and transformed.
One story warns us where unrepented sin can lead.
The other shows us what saving grace can accomplish.
And perhaps this is where the story stops being ancient history and becomes personal.
Because some of us have been chasing crowns we were never meant to wear.
The crown of always being right.
The crown of being admired.
The crown of controlling the family.
The crown of having the last word.
The crown of never apologizing.
The crown of proving that the people who doubted us were wrong.
And we have sacrificed peace, relationships, integrity, and spiritual health trying to keep those crowns on our heads.
But what if the greatest victory in your life will not be winning another argument?
What if it will be surrendering your pride?
What if your healing begins with an apology you have avoided for years?
What if the freedom you are praying for begins when you stop protecting the sin that has imprisoned you?
Jesus said in Luke 9:23 that whoever would follow Him must deny himself, take up his cross daily, and follow Him.
Not enthrone himself.
Deny himself.
Not worship personal ambition.
Follow Christ.
And maybe someone reading this right now needs to hear something that pride has made almost impossible to accept.
You do not have to win every battle to be loved by God.
You do not have to destroy the people who hurt you to prove that your pain was real.
You do not have to become powerful enough that no one can ever reject you again.
Your worth is not determined by a throne, a title, an inheritance, a family name, or the approval of people.
For those who belong to Christ, their identity is rooted in the Savior who died and rose again.
And no earthly crown can compare with that.
You can simply write, "Jesus, change my heart."
Not because a public comment earns forgiveness. It does not.
Not because you owe strangers the details of your private struggles. You do not.
But because sometimes a simple, sincere confession becomes the beginning of an honest conversation, a request for prayer, or a testimony that encourages someone else to turn toward Christ.
And if you have been wounded by family betrayal, you can comment, "Christ is still healing me."
Someone else reading those words may realize they are not alone.
Perhaps you know a brother who has stopped speaking to his sister over an inheritance.
A parent whose family has been divided by money.
A friend who is losing himself to ambition.
Or a believer who needs to remember that being successful is not the same as being faithful.
Not merely to increase its reach, but because biblical truth deserves to be carried into conversations where bitterness, greed, and spiritual confusion have become normal.
There may come a day when you are tempted to repay betrayal with betrayal, to sacrifice integrity for opportunity, or to confuse God's favor with worldly success.
On that day, remember Abimelech.
Remember Jotham.
Remember the bramble that promised shade and produced fire.
And remember the King who wore a crown of thorns so that sinners could receive mercy.
Invite your family, friends, struggling believers, those who have grown distant from church, and even those still exploring faith to follow along.
We are not here to pretend that every biblical story is comfortable.
We are here to let the whole counsel of Scripture confront us, lead us to repentance, strengthen our faith, and continually point us back to Jesus Christ.
And for those who want to help this ministry continue and grow, I want to extend a personal invitation.
For those who choose to give from a heart of worship, that support can be an expression of generosity and an offering toward ministry.
But I want to be careful about something important.
The New Testament teaches us to give willingly, not under pressure or compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver (2 Corinthians 9:7).
If your church and family depend on your financial faithfulness, honor those responsibilities.
It helps sustain the work and creates room to develop more resources, reach more readers, and continue proclaiming the Gospel.
These items are simply expressions of appreciation and opportunities to keep encouraging faith in everyday life. The discount is not the reason we preach Christ.
Jesus is.
We want biblical nourishment to remain accessible, including to people who may never be able to contribute financially.
Pray for the ministry.
Read and apply God's Word.
Help a hurting person encounter the truth and hope of Jesus.
Because the purpose is not to build an earthly kingdom around a ministry.
The purpose is to glorify the King whose kingdom will never end.
And that brings us back to Abimelech.
A man who believed the greatest thing he could do was become king.
A man who used family connections, money, manipulation, and murder to secure a throne.
A man who gained power but never gained the security he desperately sought.
A man whose final moments revealed that even death had not freed him from his obsession with reputation.
His story forces us to confront a question that cannot be answered by wealth, popularity, influence, or religious appearances.
Who is truly sitting on the throne of your heart?
If it is pride, pride will demand sacrifices.
If it is greed, greed will never be satisfied.
If it is bitterness, bitterness will keep asking for another victim.
If it is the approval of people, you will spend your life trying to control what they think of you.
But if Jesus Christ is your Lord, you are being called into something entirely different.
Not a life without suffering.
Not a life where every family conflict disappears overnight.
Not a life where every earthly injustice is immediately corrected.
But a life in which grace teaches you to renounce ungodliness, love truth, pursue righteousness, forgive as you have been forgiven, and trust the final judgment to God.
Titus 2:11–12 reminds us that the grace of God brings salvation and trains us to live differently.
Grace is not simply God overlooking the past.
It is God redeeming sinners and transforming the way they live.
And the risen Jesus is still calling people to repentance and faith.
So if your heart has become hard, come to Him.
If ambition has made you cruel, repent.
If greed has divided your family, seek to make things right.
If betrayal has wounded you, bring that wound before the Savior who understands suffering and injustice.
If you have spent years trying to build a kingdom around yourself, lay down your crown.
Because the throne of your heart was never meant to belong to your pride.
It belongs to the One who created you, who knows you completely, and who gave His life to save sinners.
Abimelech's story ended with a crushed skull and a ruined kingdom.
But the story of Jesus did not end at the cross.
On the third day, He rose again.
And because He lives, repentance is not the end of hope.
It is the doorway through which we turn from our sin and receive the mercy of the living Christ.
That is the Gospel.
That is the invitation.
And that is why our message will always be greater than the darkest scandal, the deepest betrayal, or the most devastating failure.
You can spend your whole life fighting for a crown that will perish—or surrender to the King who wore thorns to give you everlasting life.
